Q: Convert a sql UTC Timesamp to Instant in Java A:

Timestamp#toInstant is indeed in UTC

convert the stored Timestamp to an Instant

Calling java.sql.Timestamp#toInstant will indeed give you a date and time as seen with an offset of zero hours-minutes-seconds from UTC. Both classes internally keep a count since the epoch reference of first moment of 1970 in UTC, 1970-01-01T00:00Z.

Instant instant = myJavaSqlTimestamp.toInstant() ;

Avoid legacy date-time classes

The Timestamp class is one of the terribly flawed legacy date-time classes. These were years ago supplanted by the modern java.time classes defined in JSR 310.

Never use Timestamp, Calendar, Date, SimpleDateFormat, etc. Use only java.time classes with JDBC 4.2+.

With zone/offset

If the column in your Microsoft SQL Server database is of the type datetimeoffset, then retrieve the matching type in JDBC: OffsetDateTime.

OffsetDateTime odt = myResultSet.getObject( … , OffsetDateTime.class ) ;

Writing:

String input = "2023-08-08 07:52:09.877Z" ;  // `Z` on the end indicates an offset of zero hours-minutes-seconds from UTC. Pronounced "Zulu". 
Instant instant = Instant.parse( input ) ;  // Represents a moment as seen with an offset of zero from UTC.
OffsetDateTime odt = instant.atOffset( ZoneOffset.UTC ) ;  // Represents a moment as seen with a particular offset from UTC. In this case the offset is zero.
myPreparedStatement.setObject( … , odt ) ;

Without zone/offset

I suspect your problem is due to an incorrect data type on your column. You neglected to indicate the data type, so I can only guess. But I guess the type is the legacy Microsoft SQL Server type datetime or its modern replacement datetime2.

Both of those datetime/datetime2 types represent a date with time-of-day but lack the context of a time zone or an offset-from-UTC. Without that context, such a value does not represent a moment, is not a specific point on the timeline. So comparing to a value in UTC is nonsensical.

The matching JDBC type for those datetime/datetime2 types is LocalDateTime — a class representing a date with time-of-day but without zone/offset.

LocalDateTime ldt = myResultSet.getObject( … , LocalDateTime.class ) ;

Writing:

myPreparedStatement.setObject( … , ldt ) ;

Do not use those datetime/datetime2 types nor LocalDateTime if you are tracking a moment, a specific point on the timeline. That would be like storing an amount of money without noting the currency.

If you did indeed use those datetime/datetime2 types in an attempt to store a moment, then you now have a mess on your hands. You will need to use a datetimeoffset instead. To migrate data, you can assign an offset if you know for certain the intended offset of the stored values, but you will of course ultimately be guessing since you cannot know the context of every row’s insertion/update.

Q: ::operator delete in multithreading A:

In a well formed program, the operations of a thread (A) visible to another thread (B), are in the strict order of the code in thread A.

That is, although the compiler can re-order non-visible things, items like atomic give strict "happens before" guarantees.

As far as thread B is concerned, the following could happen

T2: v1=A.read(relaxed)
T1: old = A.read(relaxed); // Not really visible.
T1: A.write(new_value, relaxed);

T1: old = A.read(relaxed); // Not really visible.
T2: v1=A.read(relaxed)
T1: A.write(new_value, relaxed);

T1: old = A.read(relaxed); // Not really visible.
T1: A.write(new_value, relaxed);
T2: v1=A.read(relaxed)

In each case, the T2 thread can see observable things happen in order from T1.

The code becomes unsafe, because the

T1: delete(old);

Is not atomic. It can have the same value as v1, and means that the value (old, v1), is acted on unsafely between the 2 threads.

Q: how to fail a task on a specific retry attempt when using until? A:

According a minimal reproducible example

---
- hosts: localhost
  become: false
  gather_facts: false

  tasks:

  - name: Wait until the service is in STOPPED state
    shell:
      cmd: |
        if (exit $(($RANDOM%2))); then
          echo 'STOPPED'
        else
          echo 'RUNNING'
        fi
    register: result
    retries: 5
    delay: 1
    until: result.stdout is search('STOPPED')
    failed_when: result.attempts == 3

  - debug:
      msg: "{{ result }}"

which will result into

PLAY [localhost] ***************************************************************************
FAILED - RETRYING: [localhost]: Wait until the service is in STOPPED state (5 retries left).
FAILED - RETRYING: [localhost]: Wait until the service is in STOPPED state (4 retries left).

TASK [Wait until the service is in STOPPED state] ******************************************
fatal: [localhost]: FAILED! => changed=true
  attempts: 3
  cmd: |-
    if (exit $(($RANDOM%2))); then
      echo 'STOPPED'
    else
      echo 'RUNNING'
    fi
  delta: '0:00:00.006119'
  end: '2026-03-28 17:00:00.791134'
  failed_when_result: true
  msg: ''
  rc: 0
  start: '2026-03-28 17:00:00.785015'
  stderr: ''
  stderr_lines: <omitted>
  stdout: STOPPED
  stdout_lines: <omitted>

or

PLAY [localhost] ***************************************************************************
FAILED - RETRYING: [localhost]: Wait until the service is in STOPPED state (5 retries left).

TASK [Wait until the service is in STOPPED state] ******************************************
changed: [localhost]

TASK [debug] *******************************************************************************
ok: [localhost] =>
  msg:
    attempts: 2
    changed: true
    cmd: |-
      if (exit $(($RANDOM%2))); then
        echo 'STOPPED'
      else
        echo 'RUNNING'
      fi
    delta: '0:00:00.005667'
    end: '2026-03-28 17:00:00.794169'
    failed: false
    failed_when_result: false
    msg: ''
    rc: 0
    start: '2026-03-28 17:00:00.788502'
    stderr: ''
    stderr_lines: []
    stdout: STOPPED
    stdout_lines:
    - STOPPED

the answers to your three questions are 1: On every retry, 2: Seems so, 3: It depends, see the other Q&A.

Q: Is there a more succinct way to convert a String to a Set of Characters in Java? A:

tl;dr

No need to define your hexadecimal digits. If your goal is merely validating text input as hexadecimal digits, write a one-liner to check that each code point represents a hexadecimal base-16 digit by passing 16 to Character.digit.

boolean allHexDigits = 
    inputString
        .codePoints()
        .allMatch( codePoint -> 
            Character.digit( codePoint , 16 ) >= 0  // Test if code point represents a character that is a hexadecimal (Base 16) digit. 
        ) ;

Or if you insist on using char type, use solution from Comment by Venkata Raju:

boolean isHexDigit = ( ch <= 'f' ) && ( Character.digit( myChar , 16 ) >= 0 ) ;

Avoid char

Beware: The char type (and its wrapper class Character) has been essentially broken since Java 2, and legacy since Java 5. As a 16-bit value, char is physically incapable of representing most characters.

The char type does work in your particular case but only because your characters happen to come from the Basic Multilingual Plane (BMP), the first 64K characters in Unicode. But one emoji could ruin your day.

Code points

Instead of char, use code point integer numbers when working with individual characters. Every one of the 159,801 characters defined in Unicode has been permanently assigned a code point number in the range of 0 to 1,114,111.

You can easily generate an IntStream of code points for the characters in a string. From there map each code point back to text, text containing a single character. Collect into a list.

List < String > hexDigits =
    "0123456789ABCDEFabcdef"
        .codePoints()
        .mapToObj( Character :: toString )
        .toList() ;

You asked for an unmodifiable Set. Just use Set.copyOf for that in Java 10+.

Set < String > hexDigitsSet = Set.copyOf( hexDigits );

A Set has no promise of any particular order, and indeed the order may even change between iterations. If you want those characters kept in your original order, use a SequencedSet in Java 21+. Choose a concrete class such as LinkedHashSet to preserve insertion-order.

SequencedSet < String > hexDigits =
    "0123456789ABCDEFabcdef"
        .codePoints()
        .mapToObj( Character :: toString )
        .collect(
            Collectors.toCollection( LinkedHashSet :: new )
        );

Or, perhaps you want those characters kept in alphabetical order. Use a concrete class such as TreeSet for natural-order.

SequencedSet < String > hexDigits =
    "0123456789ABCDEFabcdef"
        .codePoints()
        .mapToObj( Character :: toString )
        .collect(
            Collectors.toCollection( TreeSet :: new )
        );

You can make either SequencedSet unmodifiable.

SequencedSet < String > unmodifiableHexDigits = Collections.unmodifiableSequencedSet( hexDigits ) ;

Mark as final to avoid re-assignment of the reference.

final SequencedSet < String > unmodifiableHexDigits = Collections.unmodifiableSequencedSet( hexDigits ) ;

Caveat

Be aware that the approach described here only works for simple text such as seen in your Question.

Some of what you might perceive as single characters in some text is actually composed of multiple code points. For example, diacriticals (accent marks), and modified emoji (skin tones, etc.).

Earlier Java

Sequenced Collections arrived in Java 21, including SequencedSet. See JEP 431 and talk by Stuart Marks.

For earlier Java, you are limited to these interfaces:

Order Class Interfaces before Java 21 Added in Java 21+
Insertion-order LinkedHashSet Set, Collection SequencedSet, SequencedCollection
Natural-order or Comparator TreeSet SortedSet, NavigableSet, Set, Collection SequencedSet, SequencedCollection

Here is example code for Java 9 and later.

NavigableSet < String > hexDigits =                             // Java 6+. 
    "0123456789ABCDEFabcdef"
        .codePoints()                                           // Java 9+.
        .mapToObj( Character :: toString )
        .collect(
            Collectors.toCollection( TreeSet :: new )           // Java 8+.
        );
hexDigits = Collections.unmodifiableNavigableSet( hexDigits );  // Java 8+.
